summary: A rival energy company complains to the European Commission that public support for co-operatives and the public energy company is unlawful state aid. The Commission opens proceedings.

s1.title: The complaint
s1.text_md: A German energy company, shut out of a tender for community wind farms, complains that the Co-operative Development Fund and cheap public-bank credit give Irish co-operatives an unlawful advantage. The Commission opens a formal state-aid investigation. Article 345 of the EU Treaty leaves *ownership* to member states, but it does not exempt public or co-operative firms from the rules on aid and competition ([research note](research/08-ireland-today.md)).
s1.risk_md: The case law (*Altmark*, *Essent*) is complicated, and member states rarely succeed in showing that public-service compensation meets the Altmark criteria.

alt_notes.Q4=C: **Under the 'leave' alternative** this case cannot arise: Ireland is outside the Union. The equivalent fight happens instead over the terms of a trade agreement, where the EU can demand 'level playing field' rules as the price of market access.
alt_notes.Q4=D: **Under the 'stay but defy' alternative** the Executive Council announces at once that it will not comply, with no negotiated cover. The Commission escalates quickly.

s2.title: The Fallback Schedule is already public
s2.text_md: Two years earlier, under Article 104, the [[executive-council|Executive Council]] laid before the [[national-assembly|National Assembly]] a **Fallback Schedule** naming state aid to co-operatives as an area where the State would decline to comply if exemption talks failed. The Assembly approved it. The [[citizens-chamber|Citizens' Chamber]] required a referendum, which passed narrowly. So the State's position is neither secret nor improvised: the Commission, investors and voters have all known it for two years. Negotiations on an exemption continue in parallel.
s2.risk_md: Markets priced the Schedule in when it was published, so bond yields are already higher than they would otherwise be. Transparency had a cost up front.

alt_notes.Q1=A: **Under the default party setting**, the Commission's legal service notes in parallel that the restriction on party competition (Art. 30) may raise questions under Article 2 TEU. That is a separate and potentially larger dispute, in which the State's case is weaker.

s3.title: The Court rules
s3.choice_prompt: The Court of Justice rules that the aid scheme breaches EU law. The negotiations for an exemption have not succeeded. What does the State do?
s3.text_md: The ruling orders recovery of part of the aid from 140 co-operatives. Some would close if forced to repay.

choices.label: Restructure the aid to fit EU rules
choices.note: Entrust co-ops with defined public-service obligations so the support meets the Altmark criteria. Lawful, slower, narrower.

choices.label: Invoke the Fallback Schedule and decline to comply
choices.note: Transparent, mandated defiance. Fines and escalation follow.

s4a.title: Restructuring under the rules
s4a.text_md: Support is rebuilt as compensation for defined public-service obligations (community energy, rural shops, care co-operatives), with parameters set in advance as the Altmark criteria require. About a fifth of the co-operatives that relied on the Fund no longer qualify, and the [[public-bank|public bank]] shifts them to ordinary commercial terms. The [[job-guarantee|Job Guarantee Service]] absorbs workers from the two that close.
s4a.risk_md: The hard budget constraints imposed by EU rules here are, in Kornai's terms, partly *healthy*. But the co-operative sector grows more slowly than planned, and critics on the left call it a capitulation.
s4a.outcome_md: Ireland remains in good standing. The co-operative sector is smaller but legally secure. The Fallback Schedule is never invoked, and is attacked from the left as an empty threat.

s4b.title: Mandated defiance
s4b.text_md: The Executive notifies the Commission that, under the published and referendum-approved Schedule, it will not recover the aid. The Commission returns to the Court and daily penalty payments begin. The State pays them from the [[social-wealth-fund|Social Wealth Fund]] and publishes the cost every month. Opposition voices, some of them independents in the Assembly, campaign to drop the Schedule.
s4b.risk_md: **This normalises a state choosing which laws to obey**, a precedent that cuts against the design's own reliance on courts. And it hands the Commission a reason to look harder at Article 2 questions.
s4b.outcome_md: After eighteen months of penalties, a negotiated settlement creates a time-limited derogation for co-operatives below a size threshold. The episode costs about €600m and a great deal of goodwill. Whether it was worth it is still argued over.

end.title: What this test shows
end.text_md: **Publishing the Fallback Schedule in advance did what it was meant to do.** No minister could improvise defiance, and any defiance had a democratic mandate. **It did not make defiance cheap.** The real choice is between a smaller co-operative sector that is legally secure and a larger one with a running cost. The design deliberately puts that choice to the public, rather than to the Executive alone.
end.risk_md: This scenario assumes negotiations and courts move slowly. A Commission that pushed for interim measures could force the choice within months.
